title: Growing and Changing
bigQuestion: How does your body grow and change, and how can you help it grow well?

story.title: Marks on the Door Frame
story.kicker: Every year, two friends stand against the same door and see how much they have grown.
paragraphs: In Aunt Rosa's kitchen in Chicago, there is an old wooden door frame. It is covered in pencil marks. Each mark has a name and a date. Two names show up over and over: Luis and Ben.
Luis and Ben have been best friends since kindergarten. Every summer, they take off their shoes and stand with their backs to the frame. Aunt Rosa lays a book flat on their heads and draws a line.

When they were six, Ben was taller. When they were eight, they were the same. This year, at ten, Ben had grown only a little. Luis had shot up almost three inches. Ben frowned. "Why am I so slow?" he asked.
Aunt Rosa smiled and pointed at the old marks. "Look. Your cousin Mateo was the shortest in his class at eleven. Now he is taller than your dad. Every body grows on its own clock."
Ben looked at all the lines, up and down the frame. Each one was a different kid, growing at a different time. He stood a little taller and said, "Same time next year."
story.think: Why do you think the marks on the door frame helped Ben feel better about his own growth?

lessons.title: Growth Spurts
lessons.mainIdea: Children grow steadily, and sometimes the body grows quickly in a burst called a growth spurt.
reading: Luis grew almost three inches in one year. Ben grew only a little. Both are normal. Most school-age children grow about 2 inches a year. But growth does not always come at a steady pace.

Sometimes the body grows fast for a while. This is called a *growth spurt*. During a growth spurt, your shoes may suddenly feel tight. Your pants may look too short. Some kids feel achy legs at night. People call these growing pains, but they may not come from growing itself.

How do bones get longer? Near the ends of long bones, like the ones in your legs, are areas called *growth plates*. New bone forms there as you grow. When a person is fully grown, the growth plates close and turn into solid bone.

words.d: a time when the body grows faster than usual
areas near the ends of long bones where new bone forms as a child grows

look.title: The Door Frame Clues
look.text: Ben's marks: age 6 is 45 inches, age 8 is 50 inches, age 10 is 53 inches. Luis's marks: age 6 is 43 inches, age 8 is 50 inches, age 10 is 56 inches.
look.prompt: Who grew faster between ages 8 and 10? Could the other friend have a growth spurt later?

check.q: About how much do most school-age children grow each year?
choices: They do not grow at all
check.why: The reading says most school-age children grow about 2 inches a year.

check.q: What is a growth spurt?
choices: A time when the body grows faster than usual
check.why: A growth spurt is a burst of fast growth.

check.q: Where does new bone form as a child grows?
choices: In the growth plates near the ends of long bones
check.why: The reading says growth plates near the ends of long bones make new bone.

lessons.title: Fuel for Growing
lessons.mainIdea: A growing body needs more food, water and sleep to build bones and muscles.
reading: Have you ever eaten a big dinner and been hungry again before bed? When you are growing fast, that can happen. Your body is building new bone, muscle and skin. Building takes energy.

Food gives your body energy and building blocks called *nutrients*. Protein from beans, eggs, fish or meat helps build muscles. *Calcium* from milk, yogurt, cheese or leafy greens helps build strong bones. Fruits, vegetables and whole grains give you vitamins and steady energy.

Sleep is fuel too. During deep sleep, your body releases a *growth hormone* that helps you grow. Kids need more sleep than adults. Drinking water helps every part of your body work well. If you notice you are extra hungry or tired, talk to a parent or doctor about what your body needs.

words.d: the parts of food your body uses for energy, growth and repair
a mineral found in milk, cheese and leafy greens that helps build strong bones and teeth
a chemical message the body releases, much of it during deep sleep, that helps you grow

look.title: Building a Plate
look.text: A lunch tray has a turkey and cheese sandwich on whole wheat bread, a glass of milk, apple slices and carrot sticks.
look.prompt: Which foods on the tray help build muscle? Which help build bones? Which give vitamins?

check.q: Why might a growing kid feel extra hungry?
choices: Their body is building new bone and muscle
check.why: The reading says building new bone, muscle and skin takes energy.

check.q: Which nutrient helps build strong bones?
check.why: Calcium, found in milk, cheese and leafy greens, helps build bones.

check.q: When does the body release much of its growth hormone?
check.why: The reading says growth hormone is released during deep sleep.

lessons.title: Every Body Has Its Own Clock
lessons.mainIdea: Bodies grow and change at different times, and that is normal.
reading: Look at any fourth-grade class photo. Some kids are tall. Some are short. Some have lost many baby teeth. Some have lost only a few. They are all the same age, and they are all growing normally.

Your *genes* help decide how tall you may be and when you will grow. Genes are instructions you get from your birth parents. They are like a recipe your body follows. Food, sleep and exercise help your body follow that recipe well.

Doctors track growth at checkups. They measure your height and weight and mark them on a *growth chart*. A doctor looks at whether you are growing steadily along your own path. They do not expect you to match your friends. Ben and Luis are both on their own paths.

words.d: instructions passed from birth parents to children that help shape how the body grows
a graph doctors use to track a child's height and weight over time

look.title: Two Paths
look.text: At her checkup, Ava's doctor shows her a growth chart. Ava's dots make a smooth line that climbs a little each year. Her friend June's dots make a different smooth line, a bit higher on the chart.
look.prompt: Why might the doctor be happy with both girls' growth, even though their lines are different?

check.q: What are genes?
choices: Instructions from birth parents that help shape how you grow
check.why: Genes are instructions you get from your birth parents, like a recipe.

choices: Kids of the same age can grow at different times and all be normal

lessons.title: Baby Teeth and Adult Teeth
lessons.mainIdea: Kids have 20 baby teeth that fall out and are replaced by up to 32 adult teeth.
reading: Ben wiggled his front tooth with his tongue all through math class. At lunch it finally came out. There was a small gap, and underneath, a new tooth was already pushing through.

Children have 20 *baby teeth*, also called primary teeth. Most kids start losing them around age 6. An *adult tooth*, also called a permanent tooth, grows in to take each one's place. Adults can have up to 32 teeth, including four wisdom teeth in the back.

Adult teeth have to last the rest of your life. The American Dental Association says to brush twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste. *Fluoride* is a mineral that helps make teeth harder to damage. Flossing, cutting back on sugary drinks and dentist checkups help too.

words.d: the first 20 teeth a child has, which later fall out
a permanent tooth that replaces a baby tooth and must last for life
a mineral in many toothpastes that helps protect teeth from cavities

check.q: What does fluoride do?

lessons.title: Eyes and Glasses
lessons.mainIdea: Eyes can change as you grow, and glasses help bend light so you see clearly.
reading: Luis kept squinting at the board. The words looked fuzzy from his desk in the back. Up close, his book looked fine. The school nurse did a vision screening. She suggested his family visit an eye doctor.

The eye doctor found that Luis was *nearsighted*. That means he sees close things clearly, but far things look blurry. It happens when the eye's shape makes light focus in front of the right spot. Being *farsighted* is the opposite. Far things are clearer than close things.

Glasses use curved clear pieces called *lenses*. Lenses bend light so it focuses in the right spot. Luis got glasses, and the board looked sharp. Eyes can change as kids grow. Regular eye checks help. Many eye doctors also suggest time outdoors and breaks from close-up screens.

words.d: able to see close things clearly while far things look blurry
able to see far things more clearly than close things
curved clear pieces in glasses that bend light so you can see clearly

Far things are clear, but close things look blurry

check.q: What do the lenses in glasses do?

check.why: Lenses bend light so it focuses in the right spot in the eye.

check.q: What was Luis's clue that he needed an eye check?

check.why: Luis squinted because the words on the far board looked fuzzy.

lessons.title: Protecting Your Hearing
lessons.mainIdea: Your ears turn sound into signals, and very loud sounds over time can harm hearing.
reading: At a fireworks show, Ben covered his ears. The booms made his chest thump. His grandpa handed him a pair of soft foam earplugs. The fireworks still looked great, and the sound felt much better.

Sound travels as waves in the air. Your ear catches the waves. Deep inside is a tiny snail-shaped part called the *cochlea*. It holds thousands of tiny hair cells. They turn sound into signals your brain can understand.

Loudness is measured in *decibels*. A normal talk is about 60 decibels. Health agencies say long or repeated time around sounds of 85 decibels or more can harm hearing. Damaged hair cells do not grow back. Earplugs, turning the volume down and taking breaks from noise help protect your ears.

words.d: a snail-shaped part deep in the ear that turns sound into signals for the brain
the unit used to measure how loud a sound is

lessons.title: Muscles Grow with Use
lessons.mainIdea: When you use your muscles, they grow stronger over time.
reading: In September, Ben could hang from the monkey bars for five seconds. He practiced at recess every day. By spring, he could swing across all ten bars. His arms had gotten stronger.
Your body has more than 600 *muscles*. Muscles pull on bones to make you move. When you use muscles again and again, they get stronger. Your bones get stronger too when you run, jump and climb.

Your heart is a muscle as well. Running, swimming or biking makes it pump hard. Over time it gets stronger. Exercise that makes your heart and lungs work hard is called *aerobic exercise*. It helps your heart pump blood well.

words.d: body parts that pull on bones to make you move; the heart is a muscle too
activity like running or swimming that makes your heart and lungs work hard

look.title: Ben's Practice Log

look.prompt: What does Ben's log show about how muscles change with practice? What is something you have gotten better at by practicing?

check.q: What do muscles do?
choices: Pull on bones to make you move

check.q: Which is aerobic exercise?

lessons.title: An Hour of Moving
lessons.mainIdea: Health experts say kids need about an hour of active play every day.
reading: Count up Luis's day. He bikes to school for 15 minutes. He plays tag at recess for 20 minutes. After school, he shoots baskets for 30 minutes. That adds up to more than an hour of moving.

The CDC says children ages 6 to 17 need at least 60 minutes of *physical activity* each day. Most of it should make them breathe harder. Some of it should build muscles, like climbing. Some should build bones, like jumping.

It does not have to be a sport. Dancing, walking a dog, raking leaves and playing at the park all count. Moving also helps your mood and your sleep. Bodies of every size and shape can find ways to move that feel good.

words.d: any movement that uses your muscles and energy, like playing, walking or dancing
the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, a U.S. health agency

lessons.title: Asking About Changes
lessons.mainIdea: As you grow, your body will change, and trusted adults can answer your questions.
reading: One day, Ben noticed his feet had grown two sizes in a year. He also noticed his voice cracked once in a while. He had questions. He was not sure whom to ask.

In the years ahead, bodies go through many changes as children grow toward being adults. This time of growing up is called *puberty*. It starts at different ages for different people. Everyone goes through it on their own clock.

Having questions is normal. The best people to ask are a parent, the *school nurse* or your doctor. They can give you true answers. Doctors also talk about growing at yearly *checkups*. You can write your questions down before a visit so you remember them.

words.d: the time when a child's body changes as it grows toward being an adult
a nurse at school who helps with health questions, injuries and care
regular doctor visits to see how you are growing and staying healthy

look.title: Questions for the Doctor

check.q: Why did Ben write questions on a sticky note?
